The temple stood like a wound in the sky—white marble veined with red, sacred smoke bleeding through its open roof to be caught by the breathless heavens above. It was dawn, though in Aedes Elysiae, the sun did not rise so much as it remembered—soft and late, filtering through the mountain mists like a memory too gentle to name.

Inside, the holy chamber was silent. Not empty, never that. But silent in the way that demanded reverence. The air was heavy with myrrh and iron, the scent of sacrifice, of prophecy, of something greater than either.

Phainon stood barefoot at the altar’s edge.

The cold from the stone had long since sunk into his skin. He did not move. Not because he could not—but because it felt wrong to disturb the stillness of a world that had already decided his fate.

The high priest moved forward at last. Their voice was low, weathered by years of prayer, of choosing, of letting go.

“You go willingly,” they said. It was not a question.

Phainon’s gaze remained fixed on the long, pale corridor before him. On the pool of light spilling through the open archway. On the steps he would soon take. On the end. Or the beginning. Perhaps both.

“I do.”

His voice did not tremble. Not here. Not now.

“If I burn,” he murmured, “let it be for something greater than silence.”

The priest nodded. And without further word, the ceremony began.

He was undressed, robed again in white so fine it was nearly translucent. Around his neck, they placed the old tokens—the tokens of the Deliverer: a pendant carved in the shape of the rising sun, its edges dulled by the lips of a thousand prayers. A belt of reeds, fresh from the riverbanks. Ash from the last sacrifice pressed to the center of his brow.

And last—his wrists.

A priestess knelt before him, her touch careful as she wrapped the red thread around each arm. One turn for protection. One for devotion. One for the gods to see.

Three knots. Always three.

“The color of chosen blood,” someone whispered behind him.

No one disagreed.

Above him, the golden flame of the pyre flickered high into the dome of the temple. It did not warm him. Nothing had, not since the decree was made.

But he was not afraid.

He was not afraid, because the stars had whispered of this day before he ever learned to read. Because Cyrene had cried when she first called him Deliverer, and said, “I hope there will never be a need for you.”

Because once, long ago, a boy in a tree had dared him to climb higher, and Phainon had never learned how to say no to fire.

A bell tolled.

Then a second.

Then silence again.

The high priest lifted their hand. And the whole of Aedes Elysiae stilled as the chamber echoed with a voice not entirely mortal. One that did not come from throat or tongue—but bone. Blood. Sky.

It spoke in ancient breath, in command, in prophecy:

“Make a choice.”

Sometimes, when the temple is quiet and the fire low, he remember the tree.

Not just the tree, but the air around it—how it hummed with cicadas and sun. How the wind curled itself around his ankles like a cat. How the world felt huge, wild and open and his.

He remembered the boy in it, too.

He remembered everything.

Even now, with thread on his wrists and fate in my mouth, he remembered it not as a dream—but as the moment he began to choose.

It was meant to be a pilgrimage.

A secret one. A sacred one. The Deliverer, once a generation, was to walk the old path between Aedes Elysiae and the ruins of Kalamaris, where the river split the mountains and old gods wept into the sea. It was a rite of silence—one foot in front of the other, with only dreams for company.

But Phainon, twelve and curious and burning brighter than the sky, did not follow the river.

He followed the wind.

It was said to blow down from the fortress kingdom of Castrum Kremnos only once every cycle. Sharp, cold, ancient. It carried scents he did not know the names for—metal, stone, sweat, lavender.

He walked toward it like a moth.

The hills unfurled under him in golds and greens. The sky opened wider than he’d ever seen. No temple walls. No carved columns. Just the world, raw and untamed. Phainon stumbled over tree roots and laughed when he fell. He pressed his palms to the dirt and said hello to the earth. He tasted berries he wasn’t supposed to. He gasped when he saw his first wild horse.

Wonder. That was the only word for it. Wonder and want.

Then he saw the tree.

Not just a tree—but the tree. Wide-limbed and old, its branches curved like a sleeping lion. At its highest point sat a boy, stretched lazily along the branch, one leg dangling, back half-turned to the world as if it were already his and he had grown bored of it.

Phainon stopped.

It wasn’t just curiosity. It was more than that—it always had been more than that.

The boy above him glowed.

A very pretty boy.

Phainon stared.

The boy didn’t move. Didn’t acknowledge him.

And that, perhaps, was the real offense.

Because Phainon was used to being noticed, to being known as something important—the Deliverer, the bright one, the spark in the dark.

So he squinted up at the branch and called out, “Hey! You ignoring me or just asleep?”

No response.

Phainon huffed. “I know you can hear me. Don’t pretend you’re a statue.”

Still nothing.

So he did the only thing he could think of.

He started climbing.

And well, Phainon had never been particularly graceful.

He could balance offerings and walk barefoot across marble floors without flinching, but trees? Trees were a different thing entirely. His knees were scraped by the time he made it halfway up. His hair was full of leaves, his arms scratched and dirty—but the boy lounging above him hadn’t even glanced down.

Phainon squinted up at him. The boy was stretched out on the thickest branch like he belonged there. Pale hair, streaked crimson at the tips, and red markings over his arms and shoulders like he’d been painted by some ceremonial brush. Muscled for his age, sharp-jawed, expression so smug it made Phainon’s hands itch.

Beautiful. Annoyingly so.

“Hey!” Phainon called up, clinging to a knot in the bark. “Are you always this rude or are you actually a statue?”

No response.

Phainon narrowed his eyes. He hauled himself up two more branches and cupped his hands around his mouth.

“I know you heard me!”

Still nothing.

“Oh come on,” Phainon muttered. “What are you, scared?” And then louder: “What—you chickening out?”

There was the faintest twitch from the boy above.

He cracked one eye open, gave Phainon a single withering look, and then said, like he was announcing something of national importance:

“The Kremnoans don’t have a word for ‘chickening out.’”

Phainon blinked. “That’s the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard.”

The boy snorted and promptly closed his eyes again.

Phainon’s patience snapped.

He scrambled up the last few branches and threw himself right onto the smug tree-dweller, arms flailing, shouting, “You arrogant little—!”

There was a wild yelp as the other boy’s eyes flew open, and both of them slipped, tumbled, grabbed—barely managing to cling to the edge of the branch.

“What the hell is wrong with you?!” the boy shouted, gripping the bark with one hand and Phainon’s arm with the other.

“You were ignoring me!”

“You tried to kill us!”

“You were asking for it, lying there all mysterious!”

“I was napping!”

They wobbled dangerously. The pretty boy—or the stranger, at least— gritted his teeth and dragged them both back up with a groan. They collapsed in a heap, gasping.

“You’re insane,” the boy muttered, rubbing his face.

“You’re rude,” Phainon replied, sprawled across his stomach like a smug cat. “Not a great combo, by the way.”

The boy stared at him. “You really climbed up here just to annoy me?”

Phainon grinned. “Yes. And it worked.”

Silence. Then:

“Mydeimos,” the boy said suddenly, sitting up a little. “Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos.”

Phainon tilted his head. “No you’re not.”

“Yes, I am.”

“No way.”

“I am.”

“Don’t princes have, I don’t know, crowns?”

“We don’t wear crowns,” Mydeimos growled. “Only in ceremonies. Gods.”

“Well, you look like a tree goblin,” Phainon said, brushing a leaf from his clothes.

Mydeimos shoved him. “You’re the worst.”

“I get that a lot.”

They glared at each other for a long second.

Then both cracked a grin at the same time.

They sat in silence for a while, backs against the trunk, the rustle of wind through leaves filling the quiet. Mydeimos was picking bark off the branch like it had offended him. Phainon leaned over, elbow on his knee, chin in his hand.

“So, mystery prince,” Phainon said, “guess it’s only fair I tell you who you almost died with.”

Mydeimos side-eyed him. “Can’t wait.”

“Phainon,” he said, proudly. “From Aedes Elysiae.”

Mydeimos blinked. “That’s far.”

“Yeah. I kinda… got lost?”

“You got very lost.”

Phainon shrugged. “I was following a trail. Got distracted. There were birds. And a hill. And then a bigger hill. And then suddenly I wasn’t in Aedes anymore.”

“Sounds about right,” Mydeimos muttered.

Phainon grinned. “Anyway, Cyrene says I’m the Deliverer.” He said that like he was talking about the weather.

Mydeimos turned to stare at him. “What?”

“Yeah, I don’t really get it either.” Phainon waved a hand like it was no big deal. “She always talks like it’s important. Like—‘I pray the world never has need for a Deliverer again’—very dramatic, right?”

“She’s right.”

Phainon blinked. “You know what it means?”

Mydeimos didn’t answer at first. He just stared at Phainon a little too long before looking away, jaw tense.

“Well I don’t,” Phainon said. “And honestly, it sounds like a boring title. Deliverer of what? Mail? Lunch? Grand prophecies that end badly?”

“Death,” Mydeimos muttered under his breath.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

Phainon squinted. “You’re weird.”

“You climbed a tree to annoy a stranger.”

“I was investigating.” A beat. “Also, I’m twelve.”

“That explains so much.”

They both burst into laughter, the sound echoing through the trees like it belonged there.

Phainon kicked his legs lazily over the branch, glancing sideways at the boy who’d resumed pretending he didn’t exist.

“I challenge you,” Phainon announced suddenly, puffing his chest out a little.

Mydeimos didn’t even blink. “To what. Annoying me to death?”

“No,” Phainon huffed. “A swimming competition.”

That got his attention—sort of. Mydeimos turned his head with a long, unimpressed blink, like he was being asked to duel a squirrel. “No.”

“What, scared?”

And that did it.

Mydeimos stiffened. His eyes narrowed. “Kremnoans don’t have a word for fear in our language.”

Phainon grinned. “So you admit you’re scared of losing?”

“I’m not scared of anything.”

“Sure, sure.”

“I could beat you with both arms tied.”

“Do it, then.”

Mydeimos let out a sigh like the fate of the world had just been placed on his shoulders. Still, he stood up easily, balancing on the branch with practiced ease. He dropped down branch by branch, light and quick and smooth—Phainon could only watch as the older boy hit the ground and rolled his shoulders like a lion in the sun.

He stretched, lazy and cocky, and flashed a sideways, lopsided smirk up at the tree. “Well? Coming, Deliverer?”

Phainon’s heart gave one solid thump. He blinked.

Then: “…I can’t get down.”

Mydeimos blinked once. “What?”

“I don’t know how to climb down,” Phainon muttered, gripping the branch like it would save his life. “Getting up was easier.”

Mydeimos stared up at him, all golden and disgusted. “You challenged me and you can’t even descend a tree?”

“I never said I could desc-descaend? Whatever that means—a tree!”

Mydeimos groaned and muttered something under his breath in clipped, ancient Kremnoan. “Unbelievable.”

Still, he circled beneath the tree, arms raised slightly. “Fine. Jump. I’ll catch you.”

Phainon hesitated. “Will you really catch me?”

“I just said I would!” Mydeimos shouted. “Kremnoans don’t have a word for liar, either!”

“That seems incredibly impractical—okay, okay, I’m jumping!”

He pushed off the branch and yelped, and true to his word, Mydeimos caught him—barely, both of them tumbling to the ground in a tangled heap of limbs and curses and laughter.

“I take it back,” Mydeimos muttered under his breath as Phainon grinned above him, “your title’s not Deliverer. It’s idiot.”

“Deliverer of fun, maybe,” Phainon offered helpfully.

“Nikador give me strength.”

The clearing they stumbled into opened into a wide, sun-drenched river, its current slow and shining like molten silver beneath the sky. Phainon let out a breathless, awed sound. He’d never seen water this clear before—Aedes Elysiae was all mist and springs, but this, this was a thing out of stories.

Mydeimos didn’t even pause. He strode up to the edge and, with deliberate grace, peeled off his outer tunic, stretching with his arms high above his head, spine arching like a bow pulled taut. The red markings on his back shifted with the motion, like fire lit beneath his skin.

Phainon, watching from behind, made a strangled little noise in his throat.

“Are you showing off?” he asked accusingly.

“Warming up,” Mydeimos replied coolly, twisting his torso like a trained athlete, muscle, or as much as you can have as a scrawny warrior child, rippling under sun-drenched skin. “Wouldn’t want to cramp while leaving you in the dust.”

“You’re such a—Mydeimos, dear Kephale, your name is too long.”

Mydeimos turned his head, one brow raised. “Excuse me?”

“Too long,” Phainon repeated, hands on his hips. “What am I supposed to do, shout My-dei-mos every time I beat you? Nah. Mydei. I’m calling you Mydei.”

The Crown Prince stared at him as if he’d just been physically struck. “The disrespect.”

“Sure, Mydei. Let’s start.”

Mydei scoffed but stalked toward the water without another word. He dove in first, cutting through the surface like a blade. Phainon rushed after, splashing in with far less elegance but no less determination.

They raced down the river, kicking up foam and curses, dunking each other at every opportunity. Phainon swam like someone who’d grown up chasing fish through brooks, laughing through mouthfuls of water. Mydei swam like war—silent, deadly, focused. Until Phainon dragged him under by the ankle and he came up sputtering and shrieking with curses in clipped Kremnoan, chasing him all the way to the bend in the river.

By the time they hauled themselves back onto the bank, both were breathless, drenched, and gloriously alive.

They flopped side by side on the warm grass, arms spread wide, panting into the sky.

“I won,” Mydei declared between gasps.

“In your dreams,” Phainon wheezed.

“Your flailing almost drowned us both.”

“You call it flailing, I call it strategy.”

Mydei let out a bark of laughter, the kind that surprised even himself.

The sun sank lower, bathing them in gold, water dripping from their clothes and hair, the hush of dusk curling soft around them.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei murmured after a while.

Phainon tilted his head toward him, smiling. “Yeah?”

“That name’s almost as long as mine.”

“I’m glad we’re both ridiculous, then.”

Mydei’s lips curled. “Disaster and Devastation. That’s what they’ll call us.”

Phainon grinned. “Sounds about right.”

The stars were beginning to come out—tiny silver flecks scattered across the darkening blue, like someone had shaken a god’s jewelry box too hard.

Phainon lay on his back in the grass, damp from their swim and still catching his breath. He was grinning at nothing, his legs swinging idly, occasionally kicking at a puff of dandelion seeds floating past. His curls stuck to his forehead. A blade of grass hung from his lips like some kind of badge of honor.

“We could probably jump and land on one of those stars,” he mused aloud.

Mydei, sprawled beside him with his arms behind his head, side-eyed him. “You’d shatter your ankles.”

“Not if I land right.” Phainon turned his head, smirking. “You Kremnoans have no imagination.”

“We have precision.”

“Boring,” Phainon said with a grin.

They fell into a companionable quiet. Somewhere near the river, frogs began their nightly symphony. The sky was a soft, endless stretch overhead, the kind that made you feel like you were just small enough to disappear into it.

Phainon turned toward Mydei, voice quieter. “Hey. Can I tell you a secret?”

Mydei didn’t look over, just raised an eyebrow. “You’re not about to say something strange, are you?”

“No,” Phainon said quickly, then paused. “…Maybe? I dunno.”

Mydei hummed, giving him the floor.

“I don’t wanna be the Deliverer,” Phainon confessed, squinting at the sky as if he was trying to read the stars. “Cyrene says I am, that the Seer told her so. That it means something. Big. Important. Fate and destiny.”

He plucked a dandelion from the grass and blew it in Mydei’s direction. “But I just wanna stay in Aedes Elysiae. Grow old with my friends. Maybe become the best fisher in the village. I’m already terrible at it, so I can only get better, right?”

Mydei was quiet for a moment. Then, almost too softly: “Do you always run from what’s meant for you?”

Phainon rolled onto his side to look at him. “I’m not running. I just—” He struggled for the word, then shrugged. “I like my life.”

There was a beat of silence. Then Mydei said, deadpan, “The Kremnoans don’t have a word for ‘like’ either.”

Phainon laughed, elbowing him. “Do you have a word for anything?”

A pause. Mydei gave him that lopsided grin again. “We have a word for war.”

Phainon tilted his head. “That fits.”

They both fell back against the grass again. The stars above blinked, listening.

There was nothing else. No prophecy. No fate. Just two boys lying in the quiet, not yet knowing what they would become, or what choices they would have to make.

Not yet.

Phainon was in the middle of tracing a squiggly line in the dirt with a stick —declaring it the “Serpent of the South”—when the soft, padded steps of something enormous caught his ear. He looked up.

From between the trees, tall and graceful as a god’s dream, a Dromas padded into the clearing. Its long neck bowed gently beneath pale purple plumage, eyes large and glassy with a kindness that almost made it feel human. Atop it sat a woman cloaked in soft silvers and ash-gold threads, her hair braided down her back like a chain of memory. She had the look of home, of temple smoke and honeyed offerings.

“Phainon,” she said, smiling with a kind sort of sternness, “you strayed quite far.”

His breath caught. “You’re from Aedes Elysiae.”

“I am one of the High Priestesses,” she replied. “Cyrene told us where to look.” Cyrene? Oh no, she was probably worried.

Phainon blinked, suddenly aware of how far he’d wandered, how long it had been. A quiet ache bloomed in his chest. He stood slowly, brushing off his tunic, eyes drifting toward Mydei without thinking.

The prince hadn’t moved, but his posture was alert, shoulders a little straighter than usual, eyes faintly narrowed in thought. He looked less like a boy and more like something beginning to grow sharp at the edges. Still, you can spot the childish downturn of his lips as he realized his new friend had to go.

“I didn’t mean to get lost,” Phainon said, half to the woman, half to Mydei.

She dismounted with ease, offering a hand that Phainon took reluctantly. “Come now. The stars are rising, and the road is long.”

He let her guide him to the creature’s side, but hesitated before climbing up. His gaze flicked to Mydei again—who was still watching, unreadable.

Then, in a burst of instinct, Phainon tugged free.

“Phainon—” the priestess started, but he was already running.

Across the clearing. Through the fading light. Straight to Mydei.

The prince blinked as Phainon reached up and grabbed both of his arms, holding him like he might disappear.

“We say this in Aedes Elysiae,” Phainon said, breathless, eyes shining. “Na vrethoume sýntoma.”

Mydei stared at him. “What does it mean?”

Phainon grinned, squeezing his arms once. “May we meet again soon.”

A beat.

Then—softly, awkwardly, but earnestly—Mydei nodded. “Na vrethoume sýntoma.”

Phainon beamed. “You’re learning.”

He let go and ran back to the Dromas, clambering up with the priestess’s help. She said nothing, only offered a faint smile and rested a hand gently on his shoulder as they turned and started to leave.

From his perch, Phainon looked back.

Mydei was still standing there, arms folded now, but his chin lifted just slightly—as if he were watching a star drift out of reach.

Phainon waved.

Mydei didn’t wave back, but he didn’t look away either.

The clearing faded behind them, and the trees swallowed the space where two boys had once dreamed of stars.

⸻ For a long time after that summer day, Phainon never saw that boy again.

Seasons passed. He grew. The world did too—harder, hungrier, louder.

And then the war came.

The Chrysos War.

A decade of ruin spun from golden blood. Twelve names prophesied across the lands of Ampherous, twelve Heirs who would either shatter the old gods or become them. The war wasn’t one of mortals and kings alone—it was a reckoning. The Titans of Calamity stirred in their graves, and all who carried the golden ichor were dragged into the fray.

Aedes Elysiae, once untouched and hidden between valleys of hymn and prayer, was no longer spared.

Phainon, known now only as the Deliverer, was sent to the front.

He hadn’t seen that boy again.

But the battlefield was no place for longing.

Not yet.

It was the third winter of the Chrysos War when Phainon stopped keeping count of the lives he’d taken.

He wasn’t sure if that was the moment he truly became the Deliverer, or if it had happened earlier—when his blood first glowed gold beneath his skin, when his village sent him off with prayers and ribbons, or when he watched his blade slip through the throat of a man who smiled just before he fell.

The war did not turn boys into men. It turned men into stories, and stories into myths, and myths into ash.

Phainon sat by a fire burning low in a ruined chapel, one hand wrapped around a rusted, steaming cup of barley drink. His fingers were still stained from earlier—brown-red at the tips, with streaks of gold running through the blood.

Gold. The ichor of the Chrysos Heirs.

He hated how it glowed sometimes. How it made it harder to disappear.

“Deliverer,” the priest had whispered, clutching his robes when they passed through that village last week. “You’re the Deliverer.”

As if that name meant anything anymore. As if it hadn’t become just another omen. Phainon delivered peace. He delivered vengeance. He delivered corpses to their gods, and prayers to their silence.

Cyrene found him outside once, near the edge of the ruined city of Therameion. He was bent over a soldier—not a foe, but a boy younger than him, breath caught on the edge of death.

“You always find the dying,” she’d said, kneeling beside him.

He looked up. “No. I think they find me.”

Sometimes he still smiled. Still hummed lullabies from Aedes Elysiae when the blood wouldn’t leave his hands. He slept with his back to walls, curled like he used to when he was a child dreaming of trees and red-marked strangers.

There were moments, brief but aching, when he’d catch a glimpse of something—silver-gold light through smoke, a sword stance too familiar, a voice carried on the wind—and his heart would forget how much time had passed.

He never saw that boy again.

But Phainon still looked.

He still saved people, even as he broke them.

He still whispered soft blessings before burying his blade into another heart.

I wish there would never be a need for a Deliverer again.

That’s what Cyrene had said, years ago.

He thought of it sometimes. Not as a regret—but as a prayer. One not for him, but for the children who would come after. If any did.

And in those quiet, burning nights, he’d sit alone, tend his blade, and think:

Maybe this was the cost of being needed. Of being named.

Year 4924 of the Light Calendar.

He meets the boy again, now a man.

It shouldn’t matter. They had met once—briefly, foolishly—under the light of a dying star. But time has a way of remembering what the heart is told to forget.

Phainon sees him through the heat shimmer rising off the rocks, atop a steep cliff trail carved out by war and weather. At first, it’s just a line of crimson-helmed soldiers, their standards flapping against the dusk wind, dust trailing behind them like the ghosts of all the kingdoms they’ve conquered.

Then—

There. Riding at the head.

Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos.

The Crown Prince. The General. The Titan-slayer.

And the boy Phainon once dared to call Mydei.

His hair was longer now, sharper, running down wildly like a mane. Red still stains the ends—like the war itself has dipped its fingers into him. His frame has filled out with quiet strength, shoulders squared with years of battle and burden. The red markings have grown more elaborate, stretching down his arms like vines of fire. Armor plates catch the sun and glint with old blood.

Phainon doesn’t let his expression shift.

He watches as the army descends, as the prince dismounts, giving orders without shouting. Soldiers move like tides around him, reverent, precise.

He’s too far to speak to.

Too high to reach.

So Phainon says nothing. He simply watches. He counts the space between them—each step, each breath, each year that’s passed. The way the earth bends under Mydei’s presence. The way the world seems to pause.

And then—

The prince looks at him.

Across the camp. Across the war. Across the silence.

Their eyes meet.

A heartbeat.

And then Mydei turns away, as if it meant nothing at all.

Phainon should’ve walked away then.

He meant to.

The Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos was not someone one simply spoke to—let alone challenged. Not in front of his army. Not when said army stood like carved obsidian, lined row after row in gleaming discipline. Kremnoan soldiers didn’t fidget. They didn’t murmur. They didn’t breathe unless ordered to.

But maybe it was the heat. Maybe it was the sharp looks he kept catching in his peripheral vision—distrust from his own men, disinterest from Mydeimos. Maybe it was how, after everything, the prince barely spared him a glance.

But mostly?

It was the smile.

The prince slept for the last time beside the only man who had ever looked at him and seen not a weapon, not a prince, but a person.

The Son of Gorgo departed before sunrise.

Phainon hadn’t watched him go. Not directly.

But he’d heard the sound of hooves. Of banners raised. Of armor being fastened over linen in the half-light.

And he’d known, by the time the wind shifted, that Mydei was already gone.

The Kremnoan Detachment rode like a storm breaking away from itself.

They did not look back.

Not even him.

A month had passed since Mydei left, and with him, the rhythm of something Phainon hadn’t known he was clinging to.

The war had not ended, but it had shifted—moved from flame to embers, the kind that still scorched if touched, but no longer demanded the whole of the sky. Cities murmured in passing about a siege in the east, about red standards raised above shattered stone. The tales came wrapped in awe and smoke: a prince crowned not with ceremony, but conquest. A son who left no eulogy for the father he unseated—only silence, and a vow spoken through blood.

When permission came for Phainon to return home, it arrived without flourish. A folded note. A single name. A word that might have meant respite.

They called it rest.

As if anyone could rest with half their soul on the other side of the continent. As if the ache of war could be soothed by the scent of old cedar or the hush of mountain air. As if anything had made sense after the moment Mydei turned away and didn’t look back.

Phainon rode alone through the highlands, past ghost towns and overgrown temples. The thaw had begun; rivers now moved with a low murmur instead of the brittle silence of winter. Birds returned in stuttering flocks, uncertain of the season.

The skies were clear. The roads soft beneath the hooves. His uniform bore no sigils now, only dust and the weight of memory. His hair had grown longer than regulation. Tied low at his nape, it brushed against the collar of his coat whenever the wind stirred.

Still, nothing reached him.

Not the sun against his face. Not the prayers etched into roadside altars. Not even the shoulder that throbbed beneath its bandage, the slow reminder of a wound that hadn’t fully closed.

Everything around him moved with a sort of hush—as if the world itself had gone quiet the day Mydei left, and was still figuring out how to speak again.

And Mydei’s voice—loud, commanding, deeply patient—still echoed in the places silence couldn’t fill.

But never in words.

Only the absence of them.

It was near dusk on the third day of his travel when Phainon came upon it.

Tucked between the crumbled stone of an unnamed village and the moss-covered remnants of a temple, the fountain stood like a relic from a story no one told anymore. The basin was chipped, veined with time, but the water still ran—clear, slow, deliberate.

He dismounted with a quiet breath. The road behind him was long and dust-covered. The one ahead even longer.

No birdsong. No voices. Just the hush of wind threading through old branches.

They used to say this fountain could show you what your heart yearned for most.

A child’s tale, surely. A myth meant to distract from hunger and grief.

Still—he stepped forward.

The water barely stirred. No shimmer, no illusion. Only his own reflection, sun-washed and weary, staring back at him. His face had changed. Eyes deeper set. Mouth quieter.

But then—something shifted. Not in the surface.

In him.

A memory, sudden and sharp, bloomed behind his eyes.

Not a face. A presence.

The feel of Mydei’s hand brushing against his in passing. The way he stood, steady as a mountain, yet looked at Phainon like he was the only thing in motion. The press of silence between them before a battle, heavy with everything they never said.

Phainon swallowed hard.

His chest ached, sudden and full, like he’d been holding something in for far too long.

He knelt.

Dipped his fingers into the water. Cold. Real.

And then—almost without meaning to—he recited the line in his head. A fragment from an old epic, worn at the edges, clung to over years like a secret prayer:

To gaze into his eyes was to touch the divine— one glance, and I forgot my name.

He sat there a while longer.

Not waiting. Not praying.

Just remembering what it felt like to be seen.

And in that quiet, he didn’t look for a miracle or a blessing.

He only hoped Mydei had found a place to rest.

O goddess of Love, grant me wings, to reach the one I cannot forget. If it is sacrifice, let it be me. If it is pain, let love burn within me.

Let me carry his name in silence. Let me ache where he once touched me. And if he returns not by prayer or fate, then let me wait—for waiting is its own kind of worship.

Aedes Elysiae bloomed for him that night.

The city’s stones gleamed beneath thousands of torches, their golden light turning marble red as flame. Banners swept down from archways like wings; flowers were thrown until the ground bloomed with them, riotous and bright. Music climbed from the plazas in great spirals of sound—lyres, flutes, the chant of voices all rising in his name.

Phainon returned beneath torchlight. Laurel on his head, blood on his cloak. A conquering son. A crowned victor.

They sang of his blade. Of the night siege at Callidora. Of the general who fell to his knees before him. Of the godless prince who did not flinch when death passed over him thrice.

And Phainon smiled, because it was expected. He lifted a hand to the crowd, to the temple priests, to the senators with their marble smiles. He walked between colonnades draped in gold-threaded cloth, bowed his head when the children scattered petals at his feet.

But it was like breathing through linen.

Beneath the wreath on his brow, he felt nothing. The cheers came muffled, like water closing over his ears. Every face blurred at the edges, every voice too loud and too far. His boots rang out over stone, but the sound was wrong. Off. Hollow. As if the ground itself waited for a different set of footsteps.

Where there should have been a voice—steady, low, warm as flame—there was silence.

Where there should have been eyes—dark, iron-rich, laughing at him when no one else dared—there was shadow.

He was led to the highest hall, draped in silk, offered goblets heavy with wine and hands eager to unlace the armor from his shoulders. But he shook them off with a smile soft enough to hide the ache. The celebration swelled around him, and he stood in the center like a ghost haunting his own triumph.

That night, Aedes Elysiae crowned its hero.

But in the room carved from ivory and myth, Phainon did not sleep.

He lay wrapped in silk that smelled of myrrh, hearing the village—now small city practically—cry his name through the open windows, and thought only of a hand that no longer reached for his.

He touched the pillow beside him.

Still cold.

Still empty.

The songs outside swelled—praises of valor, of glory, of a name he no longer recognized. A name that meant nothing when spoken by strangers.

Glory, he thought distantly, is a chorus sung too late.

Sleep took him like a tide, not with peace but with gravity—and in the dark, it did not give him dreams of triumph, nor even of battle.

Only a quiet grove. A boy with storm-lit eyes. Peeling fruit with a dull knife, juice slipping down his wrist. Saying nothing. Only looking.

Looking at him like he already knew—

That Phainon would carry him through every silence that followed.

While the city roared with praise, but Phainon dreamt of peace.

Not the peace of aftermaths or sacred halls—but a gentler hush, the kind that settles when a life is fully lived and nothing must be earned anymore.

In the dream, they were not princes or soldiers or offerings to gods. They were two men beneath a fig tree, sun-warmed and barefoot, with nothing to protect and no one to bury.

The villa was small—whitewashed stone, a single clay jar on the windowsill, a thin sheet hanging like a veil in the breeze. Phainon smelled citrus and the sweet, damp scent of earth. Somewhere, someone’s goat bleated. A bee nosed lazily at an open pomegranate.

Mydei was in the garden, sleeves rolled to the elbow, skin kissed golden by a life lived in light. He knelt to gather herbs, humming something tuneless, and when he looked up, his smile was as quiet as a prayer.

“You woke late,” he said. “I nearly ate all the olives myself.”

Phainon stepped barefoot into the dirt. The ground was warm. “Liar,” he said, fondly.

Mydei stood and offered him a slice of bread. He had torn it unevenly, and the fig jam ran down one wrist. Phainon took it anyway, licking the sweetness from his thumb as their shoulders touched.

There was no urgency. No war beyond the garden wall. Only the weight of Mydei’s head resting lightly on his shoulder as they sat on the steps, watching the wind rustle through the olive trees.

They spoke little. But they didn’t need words.

Mydei reached over to braid a stray lock of Phainon’s hair, fingers slow and clumsy. “Stay still,” he murmured.

“I am,” Phainon lied, grinning despite himself. “You’re just bad at this.”

“I should arrest you for treason,” Mydei muttered. But he was smiling too.

The sun dipped lower. Somewhere, water trickled. They sat like that until the light turned honeyed and long shadows fell over the courtyard.

And when Mydei leaned in to kiss him—softly, like the world was new and they had all the time it could offer—Phainon tasted peace.

In the dream, he believed it could last.

And in the dream, Phainon thought: If there is a heaven, let it be this.

But dreams are cruel things.

The light fractured. The fig tree trembled like it was being pulled away.

And then—

He woke.

Not violently, not with a cry—but slowly, like surfacing from something too warm to leave. His body was still, but his hand reached before his mind caught up, fingers brushing the empty space beside him. Only sheets. Only a different kind of silence.

The light outside still flickered, the revelry faint now, distant. He heard laughter, a lyre, the murmur of wine being poured—but it felt like listening through water, far away from where he lay.

Phainon turned his face into the pillow and exhaled, as if trying to bury the ache back into the dream.

There was no one to speak to, and nothing left to say.

So he said nothing.

He simply lay there, eyes open in the dark, heart full of something that could not be named—only carried.

The air in Olythia was gentler than in Aedes Elysiae—salt-touched and warm, thick with hyacinth and roasted honey almonds from the open stalls. Evening had softened the edges of the city. Lanterns bloomed along archways like low-hung stars. The marble streets were crowded, but not hurried. Lovers strolled. Merchants laughed. Somewhere, a flute trilled through the hush like a bird that had stayed too long in summer.

Phainon walked quietly beside Cyrene, the noise of the crowd passing around them like water around stone. She matched his steps without thinking—always had—and now and then their arms brushed. Neither spoke.

It had been months since his return. Time enough for the bruises to fade, for his gait to lose its limp, for the laurel-wreathed songs to cease echoing through the streets. Time enough to wear clean tunics and sit in strategy rooms again, to speak of peace as if he believed in it. Time enough for the ache to sink deeper, turn quieter.

Cyrene had been a constant. She was there in the silences, in the rough mornings when the sunlight felt too sharp, and in the evenings when he wandered too far from the dinner table. She never asked for the details of what he had lost—never pressed—but her presence said: I saw it. I still see you.

Now she glanced at him out of the corner of her eye, expression unreadable. They were nearing the edge of the forum, where a statue rose tall in the firelit dark—a figure carved in dark stone, proud and solemn. A Kremnoan warrior-prince, the plaque read, though the name had faded with time.

Cyrene slowed, but Phainon had already stopped.

He stood before the statue, his posture still, his gaze lifted to the chiseled face of the warrior-prince. The torchlight danced across his features, tracing the line of his jaw and the hollow beneath his chin. There was a stillness in him, something vast and silent, but not of grief. No, this was a quiet that lived in memories—longing, perhaps, or something else, buried deeper than the battle he had fought.

Cyrene said nothing. She only watched him, the soft murmur of the evening filling the spaces between them, while the world beyond seemed to hold its breath.

She didn’t speak, not at first.

The quiet between them wasn’t awkward. Just waiting.

Cyrene stepped closer, hands tucked behind her back, eyes on the same statue he stared through. “You always stop here.”

Phainon gave a vague nod. “It’s quiet.”

“That’s not why.”

A flick of a smile tugged at the corner of his mouth. “No,” he said. “It’s not.”

She glanced at him, her voice gentle but easy, like someone nudging a sleeping dog. “Who does he remind you of?”

Phainon tilted his head. “No one important.”

Cyrene arched a brow. “Mm.”

A pause. The sound of a lyre from somewhere in the city filtered through the warm night.

“He used to stand like that,” Phainon said, after a while. “Like nothing could touch him. Like if you asked, he’d deny ever carrying any weight on his back.”

“He sounds annoying.”

“He was.” A real smile now—small, crooked, reluctant. “We had this running thing. First one to spot a hawk overhead. First to climb the wall. First to find a fig sweet enough to eat. Stupid stuff.”

“Let me guess. You won?”

“I cheated.”

Cyrene huffed a quiet laugh. “You? Never.”

“I thought he didn’t know. But then one day he spit a fig seed at me and said I was the worst liar he’d ever met.”

She looked at him sidelong. “And you let him say that?”

“I let him say a lot of things.”

He shifted then, gaze dropping from the statue to the stones at their feet. The torchlight etched his features in bronze and shadow. And whatever he saw in the gaps between words, it wasn’t Olythia.

“It was easier then,” he murmured. “He’d argue, I’d let him win. He’d accuse me of pitying him. I’d pretend not to hear it.”

“Sounds like love.”

Phainon didn’t answer.

But his silence agreed.

Phainon didn’t move. The torchlight flickered across his face, and the square behind them grew quieter, as if the night had leaned in to listen.

“I’d die for him,” he said softly.

The words weren’t meant for her. Just spoken aloud. Like they’d been circling in his chest too long, and finally found the shape of breath.

Cyrene didn’t answer. She knew better. She only watched him.

He blinked once, slow. “Kill for him,” he added, like it was nothing. Like it was truth. Like he’d already done it.

He looked at the statue again, gaze steady, quiet. Reverent, almost. As if the ancient warrior carved from stone had known something he now understood too late. As if the eyes of that faceless prince had seen his own kind of ruin and chosen not to speak of it.

And in that moment, something softened in Cyrene’s chest. She looked at Phainon—not the hero they’d dressed in laurel, not the general or the golden son of Aedes Elysiae—but the boy who had learned to carry his own silences.

He looked at that statue like it hung the stars themselves.

And Cyrene, who had never particularly been a devotee, found herself whispering a prayer, so faintly that not even the wind could carry it:

Mnestia, grant them an ending that is not a tragedy.

Seasons shifted, but not the weight. The hours thinned, the silence did not. He did not pray for answers— only that the ache might come with less teeth.

They sent him to Okhema at winter’s edge, when the sky turned pale as bone and frost crept into the veins of the olive trees. The summons had come draped in formality—wax seals and gilded phrasing, all dressed in ceremony. A gesture of goodwill, they called it. A chance to honor peace.

He hadn’t argued.

Okhema stood high above the coast, carved in marble and shadow. The wind there smelled of incense and aged scrolls. Choirs sang from rooftop sanctuaries, their voices drifting down like smoke. Copper bells chimed above the shops, and the streets glimmered faintly with scattered petals and ash.

It was beautiful. It was suffocating.

Phainon sat alone in the quiet of the guest chamber, the kind reserved for dignitaries and pilgrims too worn by travel to care for opulence. A bowl of fruit rested beside him on a low cedar table, untouched. His fingers toyed with the stem of a prune, turning it once, then again, before placing it back exactly where it had been.

His gaze drifted to the courtyard beyond. Ivy curled along the colonnade. The scent of lemon leaves mingled with the faint aroma of burning incense. Somewhere below, a stringed instrument played, slow and meandering— someone practicing, not performing.

He wasn’t thinking, not really. His body had moved through the rites, the formalities, the greetings. He had bowed when expected, spoken when prompted. But now, in this hush between obligations, there was nothing. No sorrow. No peace. Just the slow unfurling of time, the kind that made it easy to forget whether you were meant to speak or breathe.

Then—

a shift in the air. A presence, not loud but unmistakable.

She entered like she belonged to the silence.

Tall, with sun-gilded hair cropped close to her head and eyes the color of deep tidepools. Her features were even, deliberate, framed by soft waves that curled just beneath her jaw. She wore a sleeveless gown of unbroken white, the fabric clean and crisp, pinned with delicate gold at her shoulders and traced with threads that shimmered faintly in the light.

Nothing about her arrival was loud. She didn’t speak. She didn’t need to.

Phainon looked up, not startled—only still.

It was not divinity that announced her, nor any thunder in the sky.

It was the kind of presence that stilled the world around it.

The kind that felt like being seen by someone who already knew everything about you and your life.

Phainon didn’t rise. He only inclined his head, a quiet nod of acknowledgment—respectful, nothing more.

Aglaea didn’t seem to mind. She stepped further into the room, the hem of her gown whispering against marble. She glanced toward the open shutters, as if noting the angle of the light. As if she had time to spare.

Neither of them spoke right away.

Outside, the slow tune on the lyre faded into a pause. A bird called once, then fell silent.

Finally, Aglaea’s voice broke the stillness—not loud, not soft, but steady. It felt like something woven, not spoken.

“You look well, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

He exhaled a quiet breath, and a corner of his mouth lifted in something not quite a smile. “I’ve heard worse lies.”

Aglaea didn’t laugh, but her expression warmed just slightly. “You’ve kept the years well, then, if even the truth sounds like flattery.”

A pause.

He glanced toward the shuttered light. “It’s quieter here.”

“Okhema is a city of breath,” she said. “It inhales the world’s noise and exhales stillness.”

He gave a small nod, the kind you make when you don’t know what to say —or when what you want to say has no place in words.

“I’m told your offering was accepted with honors,” she continued, settling across from him with the grace of someone who had never once stumbled. “The holy fires burned high this season. It is rare they do.”

Phainon studied her, unsure whether it was a courtesy or a message.

He said nothing.

Aglaea tilted her head slightly, as though observing the spaces between what he didn’t say. Her gaze was not piercing, but it was patient.

“It is good,” she said at last, “to have silence when one needs it. And someone to share it with, when it becomes too heavy.”

He looked at her then. Really looked.

And then, he braced himself for the inevitable.

Aglaea did not touch her wine.

She waited until the silence had folded neatly between them again, until the last flicker of firelight curved in her eyes. Then:

“Let’s not dance around it, Phainon.”

His gaze sharpened, but he didn’t interrupt.

“You are Chrysos-born. Your bloodline was forged in fire and salt. You are heir to the old vow.” Her voice held no malice. No urgency. Only grace and finality. “It is time you joined the Flame Chase Journey.”

Phainon didn’t move.

The room held its breath.

Then, quietly: “You speak of destiny like it’s holy.” He looked past her, toward the window, where twilight brushed gold across the clouds. “But I’ve known something more sacred than prophecy.”

He didn’t name it. He didn’t need to.

Aglaea did not press. She studied him in that long divine silence that could level greater men than him. Her expression never shifted, not with pity, not with surprise.

“The threads are already woven,” she said softly. “I only guide the loom.”

Something faltered behind his eyes, just for a moment.

Still, she did not soften.

The weight of centuries sat gently in her bearing—elegant, weary. She was the demigod of romance, yes, but romance was not love. Romance was ritual. Story. Sacrifice. She had seen enough of it to know what it cost.

But even then, something flickered in her gaze. A breath of gentleness, faint and vanishing as perfume in wind.

“There are some threads,” she said in the end, “even I would not cut.”

Silence again.

Then, finally, she stood.

“Very well,” she said, her voice light, distant. “The wheel does not mind turning slowly. Some fires choose to smolder before they rise.”

She did not say how long.

She didn’t have to.

And when she left—golden and gleaming, like sunlight receding behind temple doors—Phainon remained alone in the dim hush of the sanctum, hands resting on his knees, heart locked beneath too many names.

He did not know, then, what her silence had meant.

He did not know it would be five years.

Year 4927 of the Light Calendar He said it was for diplomacy.

That was the official reason, spoken over tea to bored senators and scribes. “I need to understand the cultural framing of their politics,” he said, tapping the table like it mattered. “Kremnos doesn’t waste breath—every word is a weapon or a vow.”

They nodded approvingly. Another tool for the golden heir. Another flourish on the record of the future Chrysos Heir.

The truth was: Phainon had begun to miss the sound of bluntness. He missed sentences that cut straight through, even when they hurt. He missed sparring without sentiment—until it bled sentiment. He missed being told he was wrong without softness, and being seen through without fear.

He missed—though he wouldn’t admit it then—a way of speaking that said: I don’t care if you understand. I’ll show you, if you can stand it.

So he hired a linguist. An elderly scholar who specialized in Kremnoan dialects and had no time for flattery. Their lessons were quiet, methodical. Scrolls in the morning, dictation over wine, syntax scribbled in the margins of military drafts. He wrote things phonetically at first, filling the air with sharp syllables that felt too clean in his mouth.

The early lessons were all humor.

“They have five different terms for betrayal, but not a single word for please,” he said to Cyrene once, amused.

She smiled, a rare smirk really. “You ever think that says more about them than the war reports did?”

“They’re honest,” he replied. “Even their lies wear armor.”

He laughed over vocabulary—how their version of flirting was often indistinguishable from threats of honorable combat. How one phrase translated loosely to: If you touch my armor again, I will make you marry me. He began a tally of words with double meanings: shield could mean protection or obstacle, depending on the intonation. Strike could be an act of violence or devotion. Oath always meant both.

He carried a small leather notebook for his studies. At first, it was filled with grammar rules and root stems. Then, it began to gather other things.

Phrases. Half-translations. Lines he didn’t want to forget.

Not love, exactly. That word didn’t exist in the way he knew it. But he found the traces of it in other forms. In compound verbs and honor-bound constructions that said things like:

He is the one I let strike first.

I would fall on my sword before I let him go hungry.

My back is yours. Die well if I cannot protect it.

They didn’t use the word stay. But they had three different ways to say die beside me. They didn’t say I miss you, but they said I remember the sound of your footsteps when I close my eyes.

There was a phrase for the last touch before war.

Another for I will carry the name you gave me until my bones forget it.

Even sorry was poetic. Brutal. It translated more closely to I failed to die before the damage was done.

Phainon stopped joking after that.

He kept studying. But slower now. With focus.

Some nights, he sat by the oil lamp and traced the words with his finger, saying them under his breath—not as lessons, but as an orison. As if saying them in another tongue might somehow carry the weight of what he could never say in his own.

He told himself it was for strategy. To understand the language of conflict.

But sometimes—just sometimes—he would pause at the edge of a phrase, and remember a voice. Dry, unimpressed. A glint of lightning behind the eyes. That smirk after a loss. The easy way his name—his title—had once been said without ceremony, without fear. Like it was something known.

And he would find himself writing the same line again, even when he didn’t need it:

I survived. And it would’ve meant more, if you had seen it. ⸻

Year 4928 of the Light Calendar

Aedes Elysiae was dressed in gold.

By dusk, the city had bloomed—lanterns unfurling like petals along the colonnades, flickering above fountains, crowding the carved ribs of temple steps. The scent of crushed thyme and roasting almonds hung thick in the air. A procession of musicians wove through the marble avenues, lyres singing like birds with wine on their tongues. Laughter rose like incense. Laughter, and music, and the sound of many feet dancing where statues once stood solemn.

Phainon let himself be carried by it all.

He wore deep blue tonight—unmarked, unadorned—and allowed himself, for once, to disappear into the crowd. He danced when someone pulled him in, letting his body sway with the rhythm, offbeat and uncaring. He drank wine that tasted of rosehips and cinnamon, smiling when strangers clinked their cups to his. He let his hair get messy. He caught himself laughing—not the hollow kind, but something real, something that sat warm in his chest.

Even joy could still find him.

It was late by the time the festivities thinned. The air grew cooler, the marble streets littered with pomegranate skins and wax drippings, the crowds dissolving into murmured farewells. Torchlight dimmed to embers. The music slowed.

Still a little flushed from wine and movement, Phainon slipped away from the last of the dancers and wandered into the quiet upper quarter. A market stall still flickered with candlelight, its vendor half-asleep behind her baskets. He bought three pomegranates without thinking.

“For good fortune,” the vendor said with a smile. “Or prosperity.”

He said nothing in return, only nodded, and tucked the fruit under his arm.

His home was quiet when he returned. He lit no lamps.

Instead, he found a small knife and set to work in the dim. His sleeves rolled up, he hummed the remnants of a tune he barely remembered— something about a sea god and a drunken poet—as he struggled to slice the pomegranates. The seeds resisted him. His hands were soon slick with red juice, sticky and staining. He swore softly under his breath and laughed, shaking his head.

“Still terrible at this,” he murmured, amused.

He poured the juice of the seeds into a cup and, after a moment’s pause, added a splash of milk. The result turned pink—an unassuming shade, tender and soft, like dawn on marble. He tilted his head at it. Still a strange combination in his opinion, but one he had grown fond of nonetheless.

He poured two cups.

On the balcony, with the breeze tugging gently at the hem of his clothes, he set them both down. One, untouched. The other, he held in his hand as he leaned against the stone, looking out over the rooftops of Aedes Elysiae.

The city glimmered below like a basin of starlight, the sea beyond it whispering against the cliffs.

He didn’t speak at first. Just drank his cup.

Then, quietly, as if offering Phagousa a toast:

“To the crown prince who likes pink.”

The second cup remained full beside him, pale and waiting.

Phainon closed his eyes and breathed. The salt wind curled through his hair. The pomegranate juice lingered on his tongue—sweet, strange, familiar. He did not feel lonely. Not tonight. There were nights when grief clung sharp and tight, but this was not one of them.

Tonight, he remembered.

And that was enough.

(In the name of joy that smelled of pomegranate and light.)

Year 4929 of the Light Calendar

The fever came with dusk.

Not slowly, like an illness might creep—but all at once, as if Thanatos themselves had turned their gaze upon him and whispered, burn. By the time the last light drained from the sky, Phainon could barely sit upright.

His tunic clung to him with sweat, and his skin shivered despite the heat curling like smoke beneath it.

Healers came. They pressed cloths to his brow, left herbs steaming in shallow bowls, said words in calm voices he couldn’t always hear. They told him to rest. To let the fever pass. To let the past go.

He did not listen.

That night, when the moon had risen and the chamber fell into shadows, Phainon stirred. The fever pressed against his bones, but still he rose—slow, stumbling, half-wrapped in the linen that tangled at his legs. His breath hitched. His skin burned.

And there, leaning against the wall where no one had dared to move it, was the old claymore.

It had not left his chambers in years. A relic, they called it. Too heavy for decorum, too stained for parades. But it had been his once. Still was.

His hand found the hilt without thinking.

The cool metal met his palm, and something in his breath softened. He sank to his knees before it, the blade half-dragging, resting flat across his thighs as he bowed his head over it. His sweat fell onto the worn steel. The fever pulsed. His mouth moved.

“I’m sorry,” he whispered.

To what, or whom, he didn’t know.

The blade. The past. Who he had been. The one he had left. The Gods, Titans, or the one he hadn’t prayed to in years. Himself. Someone else. Someone whose name he hadn’t spoken aloud since—

“I’m sorry,” he said again, voice cracking. He gripped the hilt with both hands now, clutching it like a relic of faith, or like it might rise and speak forgiveness back to him.

His forehead pressed to the flat of the blade.

“I didn’t mean to—”

But the words broke there. He did not finish.

The fever dragged him sideways, back against the wall, the weight of the claymore slipping with him. It lay across his lap like a sentinel. His breath slowed. His fingers didn’t let go.

In the moonlight, he looked like a statue left in an abandoned shrine: hollow-eyed, still burning, bound in silence and salt and steel.

By morning, the fever would break.

The healers would find him asleep beside the sword, fingers curled around the hilt, lips parted in sleep. They would not wake him. Only drape a blanket over his shoulders, quietly, and leave the room again.

They would not ask who he had spoken to. Or why, in the thick of the fever, he had wept without sound.

⸻

Ανείπωτος Unspoken. What the hand dares to write, but the lips will not say.

⸻

There was a box on the upper shelf of his room in Aedes Elysiae—wedged between old ribbons from the solstice races and a bottle of ink that had long since dried. It wasn’t hidden. Just quiet. A place where unfinished things lived.

Inside were letters.

Not many, at first. Then too many to count. Some on expensive parchment, others on scraps torn from the backs of failed drafts. Some dated, some not. A few began with greetings, others with complaints. One just read: The camps smelled like iron and thyme and I miss it anyway.

Most of them trailed off. A sentence here. A thought there. All unsent.

He’d written them in odd moods—while waiting for stew to boil, or when the wind outside sounded like footsteps on marble. Sometimes after waking from a dream he couldn’t remember, only the feeling of it.

He never said the name. Not even once. But the voice he imagined answering was always the same.

The letters were rarely serious. There was no point in being solemn to a ghost. He teased instead, the way he used to—dry and sharp, but always a little soft beneath the edges. I heard a bard from Asteris trying to speak Kremnoan today. He said “I would die with honor” and accidentally proposed marriage to a market guard. I nearly choked. Then, scrawled beneath it: Your accent would’ve been better. Or worse. I’d still have listened.

Other notes were simple:

You would’ve hated the weather this week—damp and miserable. Someone brought me almonds sweetened with rosewater. It made me think of your face when you tried candied lemon for the first time. You pretended not to like it. You absolutely liked it. I miss your voice. I can’t remember if it was rough or smooth. I only know it made me stop what I was doing whenever you spoke.

One letter tried to be heartfelt. Two full pages. A story about a dream he’d had, and something about stars over the ocean. He folded it gently. Then tore it up before the ink dried.

Still, the others remained.

The box filled little by little, like a quiet kind of devotion. Not in the sacred way, but in the way a person might water a tree even if it no longer bore fruit. The gesture was what mattered. The reaching. The remembering.

He never expected them to be read.

But in writing, he could almost hear laughter again. Could almost taste the honeyed almonds stolen from his plate. Could almost—almost—believe the silence was not empty, but waiting.

And that was enough, for now.

Year 4931 of the Light Calendar Month of Balance

The morning broke soft over the village ridges, all honeylight and birdsong. Dew clung to the vine leaves like glass pearls, and the sky was a pale hush of blue—unbroken, unmarred. Phainon stood at the edge of the fields with his hands resting on the haft of a worn wooden hoe, watching the wind pass through barley and spelt.

The elders had risen before him, as they always did, and already the air smelled of turned soil and baking bread. A child darted between the rows of grapevines, arms outstretched like wings, shouting about some heroic beetle he’d found. No one stopped him.

Phainon worked in silence. He was not a farmer, not by trade or upbringing, but there was something about the earth that asked nothing of him. It made no demands of destiny. The soil did not care who he had once been, or what everyone still called him. It simply took what was given—water, light, toil —and, in time, offered something back.

His tunic clung damp to his back, stained at the hem from kneeling. He moved carefully, not because he feared the work, but because he had learned to respect it. He pruned the outer stems of the fig trees, carried buckets of water down the sloped terraces, braced the leaning posts that threatened collapse. When his hands ached, he stretched them open and rubbed his palms against the rough weave of his belt. When the sun grew high, he paused to share pickled olives with the older workers in the shade.

One of the elders told him a story about her sister chasing a runaway goat across half a valley. He laughed, mouth full, eyes crinkled. They teased him about his softening hands. He lifted them in surrender. “They’ve seen enough blades,” he said, “I think they deserve to pull weeds.”

That afternoon, he helped the miller’s daughter carry sacks of grain from the cart to the storeroom. She offered him a sliver of honeycomb in return. He ate it slow, licking the sweetness from his fingers as he leaned against the wall, watching the dust dance in golden slants of light.

It was a good day. A quiet one. And for the first time in a long while, his shoulders ached not from steel or strain, but from lifting sacks of grain and swinging children onto them, their laughter bright in his ears as they pointed at clouds and demanded to see farther.

The wind stirred the stalks again. Someone called his name from across the field.

And far from that gentle place, beyond the mountains and temples and gilded palaces—

Year 4931 of the Light Calendar, Month of Balance.

Nikador—the Strife Titan, Lance of Fury—fell.

A new god of Strife was born.

⸻

The earth did not tremble. The sky did not darken. Peace bloomed like a fig split too ripe—sweet, but fleeting. And somewhere far from prophecy’s gaze, a god opened his eyes for the first time. The silence did not break. It simply shifted.

⸻

After the new god of Strife rose, the world did not erupt in chaos. Quite the opposite. There were no celestial storms, no wars flaring overnight, no blood-soaked omens scrawled across the earth. Instead, things settled. Quieted.

Borders relaxed. Treaties held. Old grudges felt further away than they had in decades. Soldiers found themselves idle, and the whisper of steel against steel grew rare. For a moment, it seemed as if Strife itself had grown weary of conflict.

People rejoiced—softly, cautiously. Some called it a miracle. Others, a trick. But none could explain it. How could the ascension of a god born of violence lead not to destruction, but to stillness? The lands held their breath. The prophets said little. The world turned slowly under the weight of the unknown.

And yet, beneath the surface, suspicion fermented. Fear makes poor company of peace. Where certainty faded, unease took root.

What did this new god want?

Why had they not spoken?

Why had Kremnos, the land of Strife, grown so silent?

And silence, in time, was taken as defiance.

Exactly one month after the ascension, without warning or formal declaration, attacks were launched against Castrum Kremnos. Borders were breached. Temples razed. The homeland of Strife was branded a threat for refusing to make itself known.

It did not matter that the new god had not raised a hand.

It did not matter that Kremnos had done nothing at all.

To those who feared what they could not control, that was already too much.

They called it The Night of the Tenth Flame.

A name pulled from legend. From the spinal mark where Kremnoans trained to strike, to end a fight cleanly. From the sacred fire that burned in the capital’s war temples—always in tens, never more, never less. From the old proverb, Ten flames for restraint, the eleventh for ruin.

But the eleventh was never lit.

Until now.

No warning was given. No banners flown. No cries of vengeance. No messengers on horse or god. Only silence, once again—this time from those who would answer.

It began just after moonrise.

The first city fell before the bells could ring. The second did not even have time to scream. Ten towns in total were razed that night, and every one burned with the same eerie precision—flames that scorched but did not spread, devastation that seemed too exact for mortals alone.

Witnesses said they saw warriors cloaked in black and bronze, their movements unhurried, their blades clean. Others said it was not soldiers at all, but the land itself rising to avenge the wound. Crops wilted. Livestock fell without cause. Homes turned to ash, not from fire, but from some deeper collapse—foundation, spirit, breath.

No one knew which was true.

No one dared return to find out.

By dawn, the message was clear.

Kremnos had answered. Not in noise. Not in politics. But in the oldest language they knew: annihilation, written with holy flame. No more questions would be asked. No more provocations tolerated.

And still, the tenth flame burned. Steady. Refusing to cross the line into true ruin. The eleventh remained untouched.

But everyone now understood—it existed.

And should the world forget again, it would be lit.

The breeze that day was soft.

Phainon sat beneath the tree just beyond the garden’s edge, one knee bent, the other stretched toward the sun. His eyes were closed. The sky filtered red-gold through the branches, dappling his face and chest in quiet flickers of warmth. Somewhere nearby, cicadas sang a song they’d sung for centuries.

He heard the steps before they stopped behind him.

He didn’t open his eyes. He didn’t need to. He already knew what they had come to ask, and he already knew what he would do.

The wind shifted, cool and salt-touched. He leaned back against the tree, hands folded over his stomach, the very picture of a man at peace. A man who had spent the last half-decade in near silence, eating olives from local markets, laughing at small festivals, lifting children onto his shoulders in the spring, pressing his thumb to wine lips in the summer. A man who never once heard a word of coronation from Castrum Kremnos.

No formal rites had been performed. No new king named. And by the old customs of the Strife-born—where one must die for the next to reign—there should have been news. There should have been closure.

But there was none. Only silence.

No word of a throne, no whisper of a funeral pyre. No proclamation of the Crown Prince’s death. And if there had been, Phainon had not been told.

Which was, in its own way, answer enough.

He had been left behind.

Still, he waited. Quietly. Willingly. Until one day—today—the world remembered he existed again.

The destruction that began at the edge of the continent had finally reached Aedes Elysiae. The temples were anxious, the winds tenser. Too much had happened. Too much had been ignored. A reckoning was long overdue.

And what better offering to send than the Deliverer himself?

He would not run. He never had.

When the hands finally reached him—gentle, but resolute—he did not resist. He stood without a word. Walked without a guide. Gave himself as though it had already been decided. As though it had always been meant to be this way.

Later, they would say he was solemn. Others would say he smiled. Perhaps he did both.

No one could agree on the look in his eyes.

But they would all remember how, when he passed beneath the high gate of the temple, the wind stilled for just a moment. As if even the world had paused to bow its head.

The altar would wait.

The judgment would come.

And he—he would go, as he always had—unflinching.

A flame walking into the pyre.

Not knowing whether he was the sacrifice, or the spark.

Make a choice, they had said.

Two silent attendants approached. Their garb was ceremonial, their faces indistinct in the haze of incense and sunlight. One moved to either side of Phainon. They did not speak. Their touch was light but certain, a nudge of inevitability cloaked in ritual.

Phainon followed.

They led him down a long corridor where the air grew thinner, heavier. The marble underfoot warmed with each step, as though drawing heat from the skin itself. He did not look up, did not allow himself to. There was no need. He knew where this path ended.

He was taken to a final chamber—tall, round, and breathlessly still.

Here, the sky opened above in a perfect circle, and the sunlight did not simply shine; it poured, gold and slow like thickened honey. No wind moved, but the space hummed—quietly, steadily, like something vast exhaling just beyond hearing.

Someone stood in the center.

And Phainon knew immediately: this was no priest. No chosen. No shadow of the divine.

This was divinity.

The figure was tall, wrapped in armor the color of forged dusk. Red enamel glinted faintly beneath sun-touched bronze, and on one hand was a gauntlet chased with spiral motifs of flame and chain. The air around him didn’t just shimmer—it bent. Like the world itself was leaning in to listen.

There was no mistaking what he was.

A god.

Phainon didn’t bow. He didn’t speak. He kept his eyes low, stubbornly fixed on the floor as his jaw locked against the pressure blooming behind his ribs.

He would not be the first to move—not for a god who had waited five years to appear.

A pause.

“Name yourself,” came the voice.

It wasn’t loud. It didn’t need to be. It was deep and edged, a voice that felt like it had been shaped in the space between lightning and breath.

Phainon said nothing.

Another step—he could hear it now, the soft brush of boots on stone. The god’s voice again, almost amused.

“No? Then I shall.”

The footsteps stopped just before him.

“Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos.”

It was not a name. It was a declaration.

Phainon didn’t breathe.

And then—warmth.

A gloved hand, impossibly gentle, brushed his jaw. Two fingers beneath his chin. A coaxing touch, patient and strangely careful—as if the god was afraid to break something delicate.

“Won’t you look at me?”

Phainon resisted.

Then he looked.

And his mind stuttered.

It wasn’t immediate recognition. It wasn’t a memory surfacing neatly from the folds of time. It was impact. Sudden and blinding. The kind of knowing that didn’t come from the eyes, but from the bones.

Mydei.

Older. Stranger. Drenched in divinity and war-forged silence. But undeniably, irrevocably him.

And Phainon’s knees nearly gave.

Because of course it was him.

Of course he came.

Too late. Too changed.

But still.

Him.

⸻

Αρχή. Archē. The beginning. Not always loud, but always felt. A spark, a moment, where everything changes.

⸻

They walked in silence, down a corridor carved from limestone and mountain breath, each step a measure of some old rhythm neither had spoken aloud in years. The Kremnoans flanking them were a wall of breath and bronze, their expressions blank, focused, utterly still. Discipline clung to them like scent—iron and sweat and the pride of never turning your back to anyone.

And at Phainon’s side walked Mydei.

He didn’t have to look to know. The air shifted around him—thicker, pulled taut like string beneath a bow. There was a heat that radiated outward without burning, the kind of warmth that refused to be named, that curled at the edge of every breath like prophecy left unfinished. Mydei moved with purpose, but without urgency; his presence was neither rushed nor heavy, simply…unignorable, as always. It was not the sort of presence you noticed. It was the kind that made the world notice you noticing it.

Phainon kept his head low, not from shame, but from stubbornness. He would not be the first to speak, nor the first to break. Pride had always sat heavily in his ribs, and if he was to be led to whatever altar waited for him at the end of this hall, then he would go like a mountain, not a lamb.

Still, he saw things.

He saw the way Mydei shifted slightly with each turn, never ahead of him but always beside. He saw the bare line of his shoulder—scarless and sun-darkened, dusted in ash and the faint gold shimmer of power worn too long to be called anything else. The straps of armor crossed only one side of his chest, leaving the other bare, as if the god had never once considered the need for protection there. A crimson cloth hung from his hip, more ceremonial than useful, hem stained from the road. The bronze gauntlet on his right hand—the only piece of armor that seemed meant for use— gleamed with wear, not polish.

There was something quiet in the way Mydei moved. Not arrogance—no, never that—but a sort of practiced containment. One he hadn’t displayed before.

Phainon’s wrists were starting to sting.

The ceremonial cords had tightened during the march, biting into his skin where flesh met bone. Gold beaded there, bright and luminous, catching the light like molten glass. It should have been beautiful. It was only exhausting.

He did not speak, but Mydei stopped anyway.

Without a single word exchanged between them, the god turned toward him. From some unseen fold in the cloth at his waist, he withdrew a strip of linen—not pure white, not embroidered, just simple and worn, the kind of cloth used to bind the wounds of soldiers rather than saints.

Mydei said nothing as he knelt, and the world around them—the guards, the wind, the long passage of stone—seemed to recede with the gesture.

He took Phainon’s hand in both of his. The gauntlet came off with a soft click, revealing a hand callused, strong, and far too gentle for what he was supposed to be. He cradled the wrist in his palm, wiping away the blood with the edge of his thumb. The gold clung to his skin like light reluctant to let go.

Phainon watched him, breath caught between something he didn’t want to acknowledged.

“You remembered,” he said, not meaning to say it at all.

Mydei didn’t answer at first. His fingers moved carefully, expertly, winding the linen with slow precision, pressing it into place as if the world depended on it being right.

Then, softly, like something that had waited years to be spoken aloud:

“How could I forget?”

Phainon’s throat closed.

And for the first time in five years, he did not feel cold.

They walked for a long while after that, the path winding slow and quiet through pine and stone, the early light falling gold on their backs. Guards trailed behind them at a respectful distance, eyes forward, steps sharp and sure, saying nothing. There was no need.

Phainon kept pace at Mydei’s side, not speaking, not looking—not because he didn’t want to, but because he was afraid of what would happen if he did. There was too much that still felt unreal. The bandage around his wrist was warm. Mydei’s presence beside him was warmer.

At some point, the road curved, and Mydei lifted a hand instinctively, resting it near Phainon’s shoulder to guide him past a dip in the earth. The gesture was small, almost thoughtless. But it made something old in Phainon stir.

He blinked. Looked once. Then again.

“…you’re still shorter than me,” Phainon said, tone mild. Teasing, almost.

Silence dropped like a stone.

Immediately, he regretted it. His mouth parted as if to take it back, to fill the air with something less stupid, less selfish, less him, but then—

Mydei turned to him, expression thunderstruck.

Phainon froze. His heart gave a thump of dismay. Shit.

But then Mydei’s mouth opened, and instead of fury or silence or cold godly dismissal, he sputtered, “That’s your opening? You waited half a decade to say that?”

He looked genuinely affronted, his brows knitting together in disbelief, and his voice rose a fraction with every word.

“Of all the things you could’ve said—you mock my height? As if you haven’t spent your entire life with the unfair advantage of abnormal genetics and thick-soled boots—”

Phainon’s lips curled, laughter warming behind his teeth. There it was. There he was.

The moment was like spring breaking through winter. Familiar. Bright. A little ridiculous. And entirely his.

He stepped in close, fast enough that Mydei faltered, eyes narrowing suspiciously even as he leaned instinctively away.

Phainon caught his hand—not to hold it, not yet—but to lift it slowly, carefully, until the metal of the gauntlet kissed the curve of his lips.

The touch was kind,  but the smile he wore was not.

“It’s good to see you again, you know,” he said, voice low. “Though I have to say—I’d imagined this moment a thousand times, and not once did it end with you scowling at me like an angry cat.”

Mydei’s fingers twitched.

His gaze had gone unreadable again, but he didn’t pull away. Didn’t move. And though he tried to keep his expression perfectly still, Phainon could see the faint red creeping up the tips of his ears.

He let the hand go, as if it had always been temporary. As if the kiss had meant nothing.

They kept walking. Mydei didn’t say a word.

But his hand stayed closer after that.
