Χώρα των Θνητών και των Θεών. Land of Mortals and Gods. Where steel sings before the birds do, and pride is carved into stone before names are ever given.

⸻

Castrum Kremnos rose like a scar carved into the earth.

All iron and sun-bleached stone, it was a city that had never learned the word surrender. High walls crowned with bronze pennants caught the wind, and towers stood like watching gods, unmoved and unmoving. The gates loomed ahead—tall, white, and closed—until one of the guards standing beside them shifted his spear upright and looked up.

They saw Mydei, and that was enough.

No words were exchanged. The gates opened, and the soldiers posted there stepped back with the kind of respect that didn’t need bows.

Phainon stepped in slowly, his boots meeting ancient stone.

He said nothing. But something in his shoulders tightened.

It was only once they passed beneath the archway that he paused.

The city inside wasn’t what he expected.

It wasn’t just harsh lines and armor-polished streets. There was grace in the austerity. Temples sculpted into the rock itself, their reliefs telling stories he couldn’t yet understand. Training fields carved into courtyards, ringed with colonnades. Towering statues of long-dead warriors and gods, chiseled into faceless anonymity. Everything was purposeful. Every line in the architecture was sharpened by function, but not without care. Beauty, here, came dressed in discipline.

Phainon, who hadn’t been surprised by a city in years, actually slowed.

His gaze drifted upward, toward the massive stone etchings winding across the nearest wall—interlocking circles and flame motifs woven so intricately they seemed to move.

Mydei noticed. He didn’t say anything at first, only matched Phainon’s pace. They passed under one of the vaulted arches, where the light shifted cool and shadowed. The sounds of the outer world softened, replaced by a quieter rhythm—the muted thud of sparring, the low chant of drill calls, the grind of stone under sandals.

“The wall,” Phainon finally murmured, “it’s… not just decorative?”

“Every circle is a campaign. Every mark is a vow,” Mydei said. “Each line is carved with purpose.”

Phainon looked again. Slower, this time. “They’re…messy.”

“They’re honest.”

He didn’t comment after that, but the expression on his face had changed. His steps carried a tension they hadn’t earlier, but not the usual kind. He wasn’t holding himself back—he was holding something in.

They walked deeper into the city. The path sloped upward in a gentle rise, flanked by buildings that grew sharper in their angles and broader in the shoulders. Homes carved directly into the rock face, their lintels stamped with what looked like familial crests. Every surface bore the weight of its owner’s history.

Phainon adjusted his sleeves. His white hair caught in the light, a stark contrast against the dark stone and bronze. A few passersby looked his way —some with mild interest, some with nothing at all. The city did not slow for him. Nor did it hurry.

He stayed close to Mydei without quite meaning to. Just enough that their arms brushed when the street narrowed. Just enough that when the road curved and Phainon’s steps faltered, Mydei’s hand rested at the small of his back, steadying without comment.

Another pause. This time at a narrow courtyard where young trainees moved through blade forms with absolute focus. Phainon stopped just behind the gate, watching the arcs of motion—measured, clean, efficient.

“That one’s good,” he said softly, nodding to a boy no older than fifteen.

“He’s average,” Mydei said.

“Then your average is better than most soldiers I’ve seen.”

“Obviously.”

That pulled a faint smile from Phainon, quick and dry. He leaned a little to the side, glancing past Mydei’s shoulder at the slope beyond. “Does this city just keep going up?”

“Eventually it ends.”

“Helpful.”

“You asked a stupid question.”

“I missed this,” Phainon muttered, almost to himself.

“What?”

“Being insulted like I’m still nineteen.”

“You’ve aged like a plague,” Mydei said without inflection, then turned toward the steps leading further up.

Phainon followed, half-laughing under his breath. “That was uncalled for.”

“It was generous.”

He kept pace, quiet a few steps longer, then let his curiosity start to bleed through.

“What’s that building with the red canopy?”

“Combat ledger hall.”

“And the one with the smoke from the vents?”

“Forge. Not open to guests.”

Phainon’s brows lifted. “Even if I say please?”

Mydei glanced over, expression dry. “Try it and see how many bones you keep.”

Phainon huffed. “You’re always so warm.”

They moved higher, the air thinning a little with the climb. Phainon’s questions came slower now, but only because he was too distracted to ask all of them. His eyes caught everything—the patterns in the stone underfoot, the way statues were half-buried in garden walls, the way water ran through narrow channels along the street edges, cooling the walkways and feeding sparse trees trained into precise shapes.

And then, without warning, he veered.

“Wait—”

“Phainon.”

“Just a second, I swear—”

He was already down the next walkway, quick on his feet. Mydei followed without urgency, but with purpose. When he caught up, Phainon had paused in front of a tall obelisk at the corner of a terrace. The base was wrapped in low carvings, spiraling upward.

“What is it?” Phainon asked.

“A remembrance marker. Names of those who died during the siege of Tareth.”

Phainon ran a hand just above the stone, not quite touching it. “They’re so small. The letters.”

“There were too many.”

Something about the way he said it made Phainon glance at him. Mydei didn’t elaborate.

They stood there a moment longer before Mydei’s hand came to rest against Phainon’s side again—light but firm. A wordless nudge.

“You’re wandering,” he said.

“Since when is that illegal?”

“Since I have to keep you from stepping into sacred grounds by accident.”

Phainon turned, expression too wide-eyed to be innocent. “Have I?”

“Twice.”

He blinked. “Well. That’s not technically illegal.”

“Do you want to be carried?”

“That’s not the threat you think it is.”

But he didn’t pull away when Mydei steered him back toward the main road, fingers still settled at his waist as if anchoring him to the moment. People still stared now and then—especially when Phainon got excited about something. A few scowled. Some watched curiously. One elderly man actually raised a brow at Mydei and shook his head, muttering under his breath.

Mydei pretended not to notice. Phainon absolutely noticed.

“Was that a disapproving elder glare just now?”

“Focus.”

“I am. On cultural exchange.”

“You’re embarrassing.”

“Then you shouldn’t have let me in.”

“I didn’t.”

Another laugh, warmer this time.

Eventually, Mydei sighed and raised a hand in a slow, familiar motion. The guards following at a distance straightened—then peeled off without a word. Dismissed.

Phainon glanced over, surprised. “You sure?”

“No.”

But he didn’t take it back.

They rounded a quiet bend in the stone walkway, where the crowd thinned and the city opened into a quieter courtyard—less spectacle, more memory. No grand statues or gilded gates. Just an arched column that had stood for centuries, worn smooth by the weather, etched with the old tongue in deep, deliberate lines.

Phainon slowed again. His gaze lifted, steady.

The inscription wasn’t immediately easy to read—the script ancient, more angled than the modern variant—but he took his time. His mouth moved soundlessly at first, wrapping his tongue around the words as he translated:

“Strength is not in the blade,” he recited carefully, “but in the hand that chooses when not to draw it.”

Well, “That’s… a better lesson than most nations ever teach their soldiers.”

Behind him, Mydei stilled.

He hadn’t stopped when Phainon first wandered off, but now he did. Head tilted just slightly, voice attentive:

“You know Kremnoan?”

Phainon didn’t answer right away. His hand brushed the edge of the pillar, careful, like the stone might flinch.

“I’ve learned,” he said finally, still not looking at him.

A silence lingered, but not the uncomfortable kind. It settled between them like a held breath.

Then Mydei’s voice came again, softer than before. Not quiet with caution, but with something gentler. Something almost fond.

“Is that so?”

Phainon turned toward him. There wasn’t hesitation in the way he met his eyes—just something a little bare.

Enough to be heard. Enough to stay close.

A basin was placed at his feet, wide and shallow. The water inside smelled of salt and bay. An older woman motioned for him to kneel, and when he did not move quickly enough, she dipped a cloth into the basin and began at his face. The corners of his eyes. The line of his jaw. His hands.

Another brushed his arms with oil—green-gold and dense, smelling of char and thyme. She said nothing, only worked the salve into his skin with both palms, moving from shoulder to wrist in practiced strokes.

“Live salve,” someone said as they passed. “To keep the limbs alert.”

A vessel of wine was set in his hand. Strong, bitter, touched with resin. He drank it all, knowing it was expected.

The food followed next. A plate of figs, cuts of cured boar, a folded disc of blackbread, still warm. No one gestured for him to eat, but the tray remained within reach until he did. Across the room, a pair of acolytes lit a brazier and burned ironroot and rosemary, the scent sharp enough to draw tears.

He felt his sandals loosened. Ashwater was traced over his wrists. A boy no older than sixteen touched a blade flat to his shoulder and stepped back without a word. The meaning was clear enough.

Nothing here was done for comfort. Everything served a function— cleansing, restoring, marking, preparing.

When the ceremonial shawl was brought forth, Phainon stood without needing to be told. It was heavier than it looked. Dyed red, lined in silver thread, the scent of cedar still clinging to the wool. It fell over his frame like a mantle of silence.

He said nothing through any of it. His thoughts were quiet and focused.

And as the last of the attendants stepped away, their work finished, he looked down the hall ahead.

The joy of the day—the laughter, the idle games, the feel of Mydei’s hand —had faded, not in a cruel way, but in the way morning fades into dusk.

This was the palace. This was what waited.

And Phainon let himself remember, at last, why he had come.

The room they brought him to was quiet. Thick stone walls, low light. A basin in the corner, a single window high above the floor, and a bed laid with dark wool.

Phainon didn’t look around for long.

The door closed behind him with a solid sound, and he stood there for a moment, eyes adjusting to the dim. The cloak still hung off his shoulders. He pulled it off and dropped it over the nearest bench. His boots followed.

He barely made it to the bed.

No thought spared to the sword still sheathed at his side. No second glance at the space. He lay back, head hitting the bolster, and the tension in his spine bled out all at once. Muscles slackened. Eyes shut.

He was asleep before the next breath left him.

Not the restless kind. Not haunted or guarded. It was the type that takes you all at once, like being claimed by the dark behind your eyelids. A body finally given permission to stop.

Phainon dreamed.

In the dream, the sky was iron, the kind that bruises before dawn. A cliff rose before him, jagged and bare, its face scorched as if by something once divine. The wind moved across it slowly, steady as breath drawn through the teeth.

High above, a figure hung from the rock. Not bound with iron or rope, but held by the will of the earth itself, limbs fixed in place, ribs rising with slow defiance. His face was turned away, but the shape of him was familiar— way too familiar. A body that bore the silence of endurance. A stillness that spoke of centuries.

Far below, someone walked the valley floor. His feet were dark with ash. Smoke curled at his shoulders, trailing from the hollow of his palms. He moved without hurry, though every step left embers in his wake. He held no torch, no vessel—only fire cupped in his hands as though it had always belonged there.

Phainon watched both: the one who burned, and the one who watched him burn.

He could not say which one he was meant to be.

He only knew the air tasted of salt and old stone, and that when the wind shifted, he heard voices in a tongue he knew but had never spoken—words passed down through smoke and myth, carried by those who had chosen to take what gods once kept.

And when he opened his eyes, the scent of rosemary still lingered on the edge of his breath.

The light had shifted—no longer the burnished gold of late afternoon, but something cooler, grayer, filtered through high latticework and the slow flutter of hanging veils. For a moment, he didn’t remember where he was. The dream still clung to his skin.

Then movement caught his eye.

He sat up fast—too fast—and nearly collided with the figure standing at the edge of the room. Another stood behind them. And another, half-shrouded in the light.

Phainon blinked.

They weren’t intruders. They weren’t armed. They weren’t even surprised.

It was the attendants again. The same ones from before—or mostly the same. One of them adjusted the folds of a ceremonial cloth over his arm. Another poured water into a copper basin with a calm, practiced rhythm.

Phainon exhaled, scrubbing a hand down his face. “I thought I was alone.”

No one answered.

He tried again. “Good morning?” Maybe. He wasn’t entirely sure what hour it was. “Evening?”

Still nothing.

Then, mercifully, one of the newer attendants—slighter in frame, with an accent that wasn’t Kremnoan—stepped forward and gave a small, polite nod. “You rested longer than expected. It’s nearly dusk.”

Phainon pushed the blanket aside and swung his legs over the edge of the bed. “You all don’t talk much, do you?”

The attendant offered a hint of a smile. “We speak when needed.”

Phainon raised a brow. “Is it needed now?”

There was a pause. Then: “Yes.”

That caught his attention. He straightened, rubbing sleep from his eyes. “Is something happening?”

The attendant hesitated just long enough for it to be noticeable. “We’ve come to prepare you.”

“For what?”

A longer pause this time. The faintest crease of sympathy crossed the attendant’s expression.

“I suggest you sit,” he said gently. “This might take a while.”

Time passed.

It must have—though Phainon wasn’t entirely sure how much.

He sat motionless as the attendants worked around him, their hands steady, their movements smooth, practiced, unconcerned. Someone adjusted the folds of a thin linen robe around his shoulders—white, almost translucent in the light, and held together by little more than a twisted cord at the waist. Another knelt to fasten soft sandals to his feet, looped with pale leather thongs.

Phainon didn’t stop them this time.

Not because he’d finally accepted this ritual with poise and grace—but because he was in complete, absolute shock. The kind that turned noise into static and thoughts into an echo chamber. His eyes were wide, unfocused. His mouth had been half-open for what might’ve been ten minutes.

No one seemed concerned.

The older woman from before adjusted the hem of the robe. Another tucked a carved token of protection beneath the belt. A third gently dusted his hair with powdered laurel ash.

Phainon sat there. Silent. Blank.

Still processing.

When he finally spoke, it was faint, hoarse. “You’re joking.”

One of the younger attendants—yes, the one who had the decency to actually talk to him—glanced up with a serene expression and the air of someone accustomed to confused nobles. “I assure you, I am not.”

Phainon blinked, slow and mechanical. “You’re telling me,” he said carefully, “that this rite—this sacred, ancient rite—involves… being witnessed during…”

A pause.

Another blink.

He couldn’t even finish the sentence.

The attendant offered a calm, if apologetic, smile. “It is considered a symbolic offering of unity. Flesh honors flesh. Spirit is sealed through exposure. The old texts describe it as—”

Phainon raised a hand. “No. No, no, no. I don’t want to know what the old texts describe it as.”

The other attendants continued dressing him, undisturbed. One of them tied a ribbon around his upper arm like this was completely normal.

Which apparently, it was.

He let out a slow, measured breath and looked up at the ceiling like maybe if he stared hard enough, the gods would smite him out of mercy.

“They’re going to watch?” he asked, his voice rising in disbelief.

“They are not meant to speak,” the attendant clarified, as if that was the problem.

“As such,” the attendant continued with that infuriating composure, “he’s made… adjustments.”

Phainon narrowed his eyes. “Adjustments?”

The attendant nodded. “You are not required to be seen. There will be no gathered assembly.”

He narrowed his eyes further. “And?”

The smile didn’t waver. “We’re to bring you to him soon.”

The attendant bowed slightly. “He said you might say that too.”

It pressed against his brow with quiet finality, the weight of it not heavy, but unmistakable. The acolyte who set it there did not meet his eyes, only stepped back and bowed her head once, low and long.

Prepared.
